Möbius: A Unified Motion-Language Model
Bridging Understanding and Generation

Jiazhi Shu1,2,∗, Chengfeng Zhao1,∗, Jinyi Wang2,†, Yubo Zhao1,2, Zhiyang Dou3 Ronghui Li2, Yu Lu2, Xinwei Jiang2, Zijiao Zeng2,‡, Yuan Liu1,‡

1The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
2Tencent Games Motus
3Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Project page: https://jiazhishu.github.io/mobius/
Abstract

We aim to build a truly unified motion model that can understand, generate, and edit human motion within a single framework. Existing motion UMMs remain only partially unified: motion understanding is handled by a language model, while generation is often delegated to a separate diffusion module operating over learned motion latents. We introduce Möbius, which brings the entire diffusion process into the same multimodal representation space used for motion understanding. Clean motion, noisy motion, and text jointly participate in shared attention, while role-specific parameters process understanding and generation streams. Importantly, Möbius operates directly on continuous frame-level raw motion, requiring neither discrete tokenization nor a pretrained motion VAE. This simple formulation naturally supports motion captioning, text-to-motion generation, temporal completion, and instruction-guided editing within a single model. On HumanML3D, Möbius achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified motion models. Scaling to 1.7B parameters and 1,700 hours of motion data further demonstrates that our framework is both effective and scalable.
11footnotetext: Equal contribution.22footnotetext: Project lead.33footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Unifying understanding and generation within a single model is a central goal of multimodal intelligence, including motion-language modeling. Existing approaches have largely followed two paradigms. Diffusion-based methods (Tevet et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; He et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2025) excel at high-fidelity motion generation but typically lack native motion understanding capabilities. In contrast, language-model-based approaches (Guo et al., 2022b; Jiang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025b) unify multiple motion–language tasks autoregressively, but struggle in generation quality. This gap motivates a unified model that excels at both understanding observed motion and generating high-fidelity motion from natural-language instructions.

Recent unified motion–language models have attempted to unify motion understanding and generation (Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026) (see Fig. 2 for an architectural comparison). In these approaches, the language model first produces a shared multimodal representation, which is then passed as conditioning to an external diffusion model for motion generation. While this design allows understanding and generation to interact through a common feature space, the actual denoising process remains largely separated from the language model. The unified representation specifies what motion to generate, but does not directly participate in how the motion is progressively constructed. Consequently, motion understanding and motion generation are only partially unified. This motivates a more tightly integrated formulation in which not only the conditioning representation, but also the diffusion process itself operates within the unified multimodal feature space. We therefore ask: Can motion understanding and the entire motion generation process be unified within a single representation space?

To address this question, we introduce Möbius, which brings the entire motion diffusion process into the same unified representation space as motion understanding. Both clean motion for understanding and noisy motion under generation are represented as motion tokens and jointly participate in the same attention with language tokens. Inspired by the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) (Liang et al., 2024) design, we use dedicated parameters to process clean and noisy motion streams while allowing them to communicate through shared attention. As a result, motion generation is no longer performed by an external diffusion module conditioned on features produced by the language model. Instead, noisy motion is progressively denoised directly within the unified multimodal space, where it can continuously interact with clean motion and language semantics. The generated motion can in turn be fed back as clean motion tokens for subsequent understanding and reasoning, forming a fully unified loop between motion generation and understanding. This tighter integration leads to stronger motion generation, understanding, and cross-modal interaction within a unified model.

A key advantage of this formulation is that it removes the need to learn an intermediate motion latent space. Rather than relying on a pretrained motion VAE, tokenizer, or task-specific encoder (Jiang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), Möbius operates directly on raw motion representations. Clean motion used for understanding and noisy motion used for generation share the same representation interface: both are projected into the unified multimodal space, with their roles distinguished only by whether they represent clean observations or noisy states undergoing denoising. This makes motion understanding and generation two modes of computation over the same underlying motion representation, rather than two tasks connected through separately learned latent spaces. The resulting framework is considerably simpler, requiring no additional representation learning stage or pretrained motion encoder, while our experiments show that directly modeling raw motion is sufficient to achieve strong performance for both understanding and generation.

To preserve the generalization ability of the pretrained LLM used in Möbius, we adopt a curriculum training strategy. Joint training can introduce interference between understanding and generation, as gradients from the generation objective can propagate into the understanding parameters through shared attention. We therefore first train on motion understanding tasks, allowing the LLM to acquire meaningful motion semantics, and then introduce the generation objective on top of this learned representation. This curriculum training strategy provides a stable foundation for generation while better preserving the model’s original generalization ability.

We evaluate two model variants to assess benchmark performance and the benefits of scaling model capacity and training data. Under the HumanML3D evaluation protocol (Guo et al., 2022a), Möbius-0.6B achieves state-of-the-art results in both text-to-motion generation and motion captioning, outperforming relevant diffusion-based, language-model-based, and motion–language baselines. Möbius-0.6B also demonstrates strong capabilities in motion completion, motion in-betweening, and instruction-guided editing. Controlled ablations substantiate the effectiveness of our reasoner–generator architecture, showing that coupling motion understanding and generation yields improvements over commonly used architectural alternatives. We further present Möbius-1.7B, a larger variant trained on 1,700 hours of high-quality motion data, which delivers additional improvements across all motion-language tasks on both controlled and uncontrolled user inputs.

2 Related Work

Unified Multimodal Models.

Unified multimodal models bring understanding and generation into a shared framework, as exemplified by recent systems such as BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025) and Cosmos3 (Agarwal et al., 2026). Existing approaches adopt unified sequence modeling (Chameleon Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2024) or hybrid objectives combining text autoregression with visual denoising (Zhou et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026). Mixture-of-Transformers introduces modality-specific computation with shared attention (Liang et al., 2024), while task-decoupled architectures further address interference between understanding and generation (Wu et al., 2026). These developments motivate our investigation of specialized computation within a unified motion–language model.

Human Motion Modeling.

Human motion research spans diffusion-based generation (Tevet et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024a; Wen et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026), discrete-token generation (Zhang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025), retrieval and understanding (Petrovich et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025), editing and completion (Athanasiou et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025d; Cohan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), and spatial control (Wan et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). These methods are typically developed for particular tasks, with objectives and conditioning mechanisms tailored to their settings. Generalist frameworks consolidate multiple motion synthesis tasks (Guo et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Cong et al., 2026), motivating broader unification that also incorporates language-based motion understanding.

Unified Motion Understanding and Generation.

Motion–language models support understanding and generation through discrete motion vocabularies (Guo et al., 2022b; Jiang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025c; Zhou et al., 2024b), with extensions to conversational and multimodal interaction (Jiang et al., 2024; Ling et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024). Continuous alternatives avoid discrete quantization: MoTe (Wu et al., 2024) and UniMotion (Li et al., 2025a) jointly model motion and text through latent diffusion, while MotionGPT3 (Zhu et al., 2025), LLaMo (Li et al., 2026), and UniMotion (Wang et al., 2026) integrate continuous motion representations with language-model backbones for unified understanding and generation. These approaches avoid discrete motion tokens but still rely on learned motion latent spaces or encoder–decoder interfaces. Möbius instead operates directly on framewise motion features and brings denoising into the unified multimodal backbone. Clean motion, noisy motion, and text share attention, while role-specific projectors and Transformer parameters specialize their processing. This allows noisy motion to continuously interact with motion and language context throughout denoising.

3 Method

Möbius unifies motion understanding and generation within a shared representation space (see Figure 3). Starting from frame-level raw motion (Section 3.1), Möbius routes clean and noisy motion tokens to role-specific parameters while allowing them to interact through shared attention (Section 3.2). It further adopts a curriculum training strategy to establish a stable foundation for generation while preserving the model’s original generalization ability (Section 3.3).

3.1 Frame-level raw motion representation

In our framework, we choose frame-level raw motion as the motion representation instead of learning any additional motion encoder. In previous methods, discrete motion tokenizers introduce quantization error (Guo et al., 2022b; Jiang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025b), while VAE-based approaches compress motion to temporally downsampled latents (Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), losing frame-level information. Instead, we follow HY-Motion (Wen et al., 2025) to represent a motion clip as X=[x1,…,xT]⊤∈ℝT×DX=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D} with motion token dimension D=201D{=}201 comprising joint positions and rotations. Special tokens ⟨BOM⟩\langle\mathrm{BOM}\rangle and ⟨EOM⟩\langle\mathrm{EOM}\rangle are used to delimit the motion token sequence from text. Two dedicated projectors map clean motion tokens and noisy motion tokens to the shared representation space for understanding and generation, and corresponding motion heads decode it back to the raw motion space. In comparison with existing methods (Jiang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026) that learn different encoders for understanding and generation, we show that the raw motion representation can achieve strong performance in a unified representation space.

3.2 Unified feature space attention with MoT

To process all the clean or noisy raw motion and text prompts, we adopt a Mixture-of-Transformers (Liang et al., 2024) structure. In MoT, tokens are routed to different parameters for normalization and linear projection but are then processed by a unified attention operation. We introduce how we route different tokens, and then we discuss how to conduct generative denoising.

Routing scheme.

We route tokens based on their roles. Text tokens, boundary tokens, and clean motions are intended for understanding and are processed by the understanding parameters. Noisy target motions are used for generation and thus processed by the generation parameters

ri={gen,i​-th token is a noisy motion token,und,otherwise,r_{i}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{gen},&i\text{-th token is a noisy motion token},\\ \mathrm{und},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (1)

where rir_{i} determines the set of parameters used in normalization and linear projection (“to QKV" in standard attention layers). After that, all projected tokens are processed by a shared attention operation to exchange information in the same feature space.

Bidirectional attention for motion.

In our design, motion token attention follows a different bidirectional visibility pattern from the causal attention of autoregressive text tokens. Specifically, we allow all motion tokens within the same motion sequence to attend bidirectionally to one another, regardless of whether they represent clean motion for understanding or noisy motion for generation. For understanding, the entire observed motion is already available as input, so bidirectional attention enables each frame to capture context from the complete motion sequence. For generation, all noisy target frames are instantiated jointly at each denoising step, and bidirectional attention allows each frame to exploit both past and future temporal context during refinement. Text tokens, in contrast, retain the causal attention pattern of the pretrained language model. In implementation, the target generated motion sequence is always put at the end of the whole sequence with its generation sequence length specified before denoising, allowing the full noisy sequence to be progressively refined as a whole.

3.3 Curriculum training strategy

We train Möbius in two stages. Directly optimizing motion understanding and generation together is unstable, as the randomly initialized generation pathway can disrupt the pretrained language representations and degrade the model’s understanding ability. We therefore adopt an understanding-first training strategy: the model first learns to interpret motion in the language space, and generation is introduced only after this representation has been established.

Phase I: motion understanding.

We initialize our model from Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) and train it together with the motion projector on motion captioning. Given a clean motion sequence XX, an instruction CC, and a target response Y=(y1,…,yL)Y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L}), we use the standard autoregressive language modeling objective:

ℒund=−𝔼(X,C,Y)​[1L​∑j=1Llog⁡pθund​(yj∣y<j,C,X)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{und}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(X,C,Y)}\left[\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\log p_{\theta_{\mathrm{und}}}(y_{j}\mid y_{<j},C,X)\right]. (2)

This stage allows the pretrained LLM to acquire motion semantics while preserving its original language reasoning capability.

Phase II: motion generation.

We then initialize the generation parameters from the trained understanding parameters and freeze the understanding parameters. For a target motion XgtX_{\mathrm{gt}}, we sample ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and t∼𝒰⁡[0,1]t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1], and construct a noisy motion

Xt=(1−t)​ϵ+t​Xgt.X_{t}=(1-t)\epsilon+tX_{\mathrm{gt}}. (3)

The model is trained to iteratively denoise XtX_{t} to recover the clean motion while attending to the frozen text and motion representations produced by the understanding part:

ℒgen=𝔼⁡[‖fθgen​(Xt,t,Hθund​(C))−Xgt‖F2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|f_{\theta_{\mathrm{gen}}}(X_{t},t;H_{\theta_{\mathrm{und}}}(C))-X_{\mathrm{gt}}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right]. (4)

This staged training lets generation build on an already learned motion–language representation, avoiding interference with the pretrained understanding capability.

Unified motion editing and completion.

The same framework naturally extends to a broad range of motion editing and completion tasks by treating the source motion as part of the conditioning context and generating the desired target motion. We also train our model on these tasks. Depending on which parts of the source are observed, the model supports temporal completion, including prediction, backcasting, in-betweening and keyframe infilling. It also supports semantic editing, where a source motion is modified according to a natural-language instruction. In all cases, the observed source motion is encoded as clean context, while the generation process predicts the missing or edited target motion. We construct diverse training pairs covering these settings and jointly train a unified editing model without introducing task-specific architectures.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate Möbius on text-to-motion generation, motion captioning, instruction-guided editing, and temporal completion tasks, and conduct controlled ablations to examine its key design choices. Bold and underlined metric numbers indicate the best and second-best performance respectively.

Text-to-motion generation and motion captioning.

We consider two model scales: Möbius-0.6B and Möbius-1.7B. The standard 0.6B variant is trained exclusively on HumanML3D (Guo et al., 2022a), while the 1.7B variant additionally uses an internal training corpus containing 1,700 hours of annotated motion. For the generation task, we use the MS-272 evaluator introduced by MotionStreamer (Xiao et al., 2025) to compare against representative baselines from diffusion-based models (Tevet et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025), autoregressive models (Zhang et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024), and unified motion-language models (Jiang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). For motion captioning, we follow the TM2T protocol (Guo et al., 2022b) to compare with those methods that natively support understanding (Guo et al., 2022b; Jiang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024).

Motion editing and completion.

For editing and completion tasks, we report the performance on MotionLab (Guo et al., 2025) benchmark of both Möbius-0.6B trained on HumanML3D (Guo et al., 2022a) and an additional variant that incorporates MotionFix (Athanasiou et al., 2024) data in training. The compared baselines include the task-specific baseline MotionFix (Athanasiou et al., 2024), the generalist model MotionLab (Guo et al., 2025), and also the unedited source motion.

4.2 Quantitative Evaluation

Results.

As shown in Table 1, Möbius-0.6B outperforms both generation-specialized and unified baselines trained on HumanML3D. The scaled Möbius-1.7B also achieves strong performance against large-scale motion models, attaining the best R-Precision, FID, and MMDist among the compared methods. For motion understanding, Möbius consistently outperforms existing unified motion-language models across all reported metrics (Table 2). Furthermore, Möbius surpasses editing-specialized baselines and even the unedited source motion (Table 3), demonstrating strong instruction-following capabilities.

Analysis.

We attribute our advantages in motion generation to the unified architecture. The routing scheme brings the entire motion diffusion process into the shared representation space, allowing the semantics of clean motion and language to continuously guide generation. Meanwhile, the curriculum training strategy helps preserve the reasoning ability inherited from the pretrained LLM, resulting in strong motion-understanding performance. Together with the frame-level raw motion representation, these designs also enable framewise control and editing that follow language instructions well, improving performance across motion–language tasks without sacrificing one capability for another.

4.3 Qualitative Evaluation

Figure 4 illustrates the versatility of Möbius across both motion understanding and generation tasks. For text-to-motion generation, Möbius follows challenging multi-part prompts while preserving their temporal ordering. For motion-to-text captioning, it captures the key actions and their temporal progression more accurately. For instruction-guided editing, it modifies the target motion while preserving the surrounding source content. Temporal completion requires no task-specific architecture: changing which frames are treated as observed is sufficient to support motion prediction, backcasting, in-betweening, and keyframe infilling. Across these settings, the same frame-level representation supports both motion understanding and flexible conditional generation.

4.4 Ablation Studies

We ablate the motion encoding, routing strategy, and understanding–generation training in Table 4. All variants use Qwen3-0.6B, are trained on HumanML3D using only the T2M and M2T objectives, and use MS-272 from MotionStreamer (Xiao et al., 2025) as the underlying motion feature format. For motion encoding, VQ discretizes motion using a tokenizer trained following MotionGPT (Jiang et al., 2023), VAE maps motion into the pretrained latent space of MotionStreamer, and Frame directly models framewise MS-272 features without an intermediate motion codec. For routing, Dense uses a single parameter set for all tokens, Modality separates text and motion computation but uses the same motion parameters for both clean observations and noisy denoising states, while Role (ours) assigns role-specific parameters to text/clean motion and noisy motion while retaining shared attention. For training, Gen. only trains generation without understanding pretraining, Und.→\toGen. first establishes motion–language understanding and then transfers it to generation, Gen.→\toAlign→\toJoint follows the MotionGPT3 (Zhu et al., 2025) schedule, and Und.++Gen. jointly optimizes both objectives.

Which motion encoding best supports unified modeling? We compare three representative motion interfaces in IDs 1, 2, and 10. Since discrete VQ tokens do not naturally represent intermediate continuous denoising states, the VQ variant uses dense computation, whereas the VAE and frame-level variants support role-specific processing of clean and noisy motion. VQ substantially weakens generation, while VAE remains competitive but yields weaker motion understanding than direct frame-level encoding. Overall, frame-level modeling provides the strongest balance between the two capabilities. Moreover, its one-to-one correspondence between motion frames and model positions naturally supports temporal completion and frame-conditioned manipulation.

Should computation be separated by modality or by role? With modality routing, the understanding-only model (ID 3) performs normally, but using the same motion parameters for both clean observations and noisy denoising states (ID 4) causes understanding to collapse. The generate–align–joint schedule (ID 5) largely recovers understanding, but at a substantial cost to generation quality. In contrast, separating clean and noisy motion by computational role (ID 10) maintains strong performance in both directions, indicating that the two roles benefit from specialized parameters while still interacting through shared attention.

How should understanding be transferred to generation? IDs 6–10 further isolate how learned motion–language understanding benefits generation. Compared with generation-only training (ID 6), the full model (ID 10) shows that establishing motion–language understanding first provides a stronger foundation for synthesis. Joint optimization (ID 7) notably degrades understanding, revealing interference between the two objectives when optimized together. Restricting denoising to only the final-layer context representations (ID 8) also weakens generation, demonstrating the benefit of layer-wise interaction throughout the denoising process. Randomly initializing the denoising parameters (ID 9) further degrades performance relative to initialization from the parameters learned during understanding. Together, these results support our understanding-first strategy: first establish motion–language alignment, then transfer it to generation through parameter initialization and layer-wise interaction while keeping the learned understanding parameters fixed.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

We presented Möbius, a unified motion–language model that organizes computation by role rather than modality. Its role-routed architecture and continuous frame-level motion interface support motion understanding, generation, editing, and temporal completion within a single unified framework. The results also highlight the benefit of transferring learned motion understanding to generation. Experiments on HumanML3D show strong T2M and M2T performance, while scaling to 1.7B parameters and 1,700 hours of motion data further demonstrates the effectiveness of the design at larger scale.

More broadly, Möbius demonstrates that understanding and continuous motion generation need not be connected through a separate latent generator, but can instead operate together within a shared multimodal representation space. Our current experiments focus on controlled single-person motion settings. Future work will extend Möbius toward multi-person interaction, more detailed hand and finger motion, retargeting across heterogeneous body structures, and deployment in embodied systems such as real-world robots.

AI use statement

Generative AI tools were used only to improve the readability and language of the manuscript, including grammar, phrasing, and stylistic editing. They were not used to develop the research methodology, design experiments, implement methods, generate or modify data, formulate mathematical claims, or interpret experimental results. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted edits and take responsibility for the final content of the paper.

Appendix A Experimental Details and Inference

This supplement provides experimental and inference details, evaluation protocols, and additional results.

A.1 Datasets

Möbius-0.6B uses HumanML3D motion–text data, while the 1.7B model additionally uses an internal corpus of approximately 1,700 hours. The editing variant adds MotionFix pairs during Phase II. Pure-text examples are interleaved during Phase I; “HumanML3D-only” refers to the source of motion–text supervision, not the absence of language pretraining or replay.

A.2 Continuous Motion Interface

We use 201-dimensional HY-Motion features at 30 FPS: pelvis translation (3), root orientation in a continuous 6D representation (6), local body rotations (126), and root-relative joint positions (66). Each frame occupies one Transformer position. Let μ,σ∈ℝ201\mu,\sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{201} denote the training-set feature statistics, and define the elementwise scale σ~=max⁡(σ,ε)\tilde{\sigma}=\max(\sigma,\varepsilon) for ε>0\varepsilon>0. Normalization and its inverse are

x¯i=(xi−μ)⊘σ~,xi=x¯i⊙σ~+μ,\bar{x}_{i}=(x_{i}-\mu)\oslash\tilde{\sigma},\qquad x_{i}=\bar{x}_{i}\odot\tilde{\sigma}+\mu, (5)

where operations are elementwise. All flow equations in the paper operate in this normalized space.

For observed motion, PundP_{\mathrm{und}} denotes the framewise mapping before output normalization and learned scaling:

zi=Pund​(x¯i),hiobs=mi​s​zimax⁡(‖zi‖2,ε)+(1−mi)​e[M],s=min⁡(exp⁡(b),smax).z_{i}=P_{\mathrm{und}}(\bar{x}_{i}),\qquad h_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=m_{i}\,s\frac{z_{i}}{\max(\|z_{i}\|_{2},\varepsilon)}+(1-m_{i})e_{[\mathrm{M}]},\qquad s=\min(\exp(b),s_{\max}). (6)

Here mi∈{0,1}m_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether a source frame is visible, bb is learned, and e[M]e_{[\mathrm{M}]} represents an unrevealed frame. Noisy targets use hitgt=Pgen​(Xt,i)+e⁡(t)h_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=P_{\mathrm{gen}}(X_{t,i})+e(t) and are decoded by X^i=Pout​(gi)\widehat{X}_{i}=P_{\mathrm{out}}(g_{i}), where gig_{i} is the final-layer hidden state at target position ii, computed using the generation parameters. The projector architectures, scale cap, and numerical constants are recorded in Table S1.

A.3 Task Construction

Let CC be the text instruction, BSB_{S} an observed-motion span, BtB_{t} the noisy target span, and YY a text response. The mask mm controls which source frames are provided as clean context to the understanding parameters. Task-specific context is summarized in Table S3.

For editing, the source is supplied only as understanding context; the target starts from Gaussian noise, as in T2M. Temporal tasks also provide observed frames through the understanding context, without pinning generated frames after sampling updates. Their observation masks and initialization settings are specified with the evaluation protocol below.

A.4 Inference

The model predicts a clean endpoint using the generation parameters. Text-only classifier-free guidance retains the same motion context in both passes. Here fθ​(Xt,t,C,S,m)f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;C,S,m) abbreviates the endpoint predictor with context encoded using the understanding parameters, and θ=(θund,θgen)\theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{und}},\theta_{\mathrm{gen}}):

X^g​(Xt,t)=fθ​(Xt,t,∅,S,m)+w⁡[fθ​(Xt,t,C,S,m)−fθ​(Xt,t,∅,S,m)].\widehat{X}_{g}(X_{t},t)=f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;\varnothing,S,m)+w\bigl[f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;C,S,m)-f_{\theta}(X_{t},t;\varnothing,S,m)\bigr]. (7)

The source is absent for T2M. For a grid 0=t0<⋯<tN=10=t_{0}<\cdots<t_{N}=1, Euler sampling converts the predicted endpoint to a velocity:

Xtn+1=Xtn+(tn+1−tn)​X^g​(Xtn,tn)−Xtnmax⁡(1−tn,ε).X_{t_{n+1}}=X_{t_{n}}+(t_{n+1}-t_{n})\frac{\widehat{X}_{g}(X_{t_{n}},t_{n})-X_{t_{n}}}{\max(1-t_{n},\varepsilon)}. (8)

The network is evaluated at tn<1t_{n}<1, and the final motion is denormalized. Because context cannot attend to noisy targets, its layer-wise keys and values can be reused across sampling steps; conditional and null-text passes use separate caches.

For M2T, the model uses the understanding parameters to generate p⁡(Y∣C,S)=∏jp⁡(yj∣y<j,C,S)p(Y\mid C,S)=\prod_{j}p(y_{j}\mid y_{<j},C,S) autoregressively. Pure-text inference uses the same parameters without a motion span. Sampler and text-decoding settings are listed in Table S4.

A.5 Inference Efficiency

Table S5 reports single-GPU measurements for both model sizes with EMA weights and BF16 autocast. T2M uses 50 Euler steps, CFG 3.0, and separate conditional/unconditional passes. M2T uses greedy decoding with EOS stopping and a limit of 128 new tokens; actual output lengths are reported because they affect decoding latency. The fixed inputs are the first eight captions in the T2M evaluation protocol and the first eight eligible M2T motions in sorted ID order, cropped to 150 frames. Batch-one measurements use the first input in each set. Timing includes context encoding and generation, with CUDA synchronization around each call. Model loading, dataset I/O, motion conversion, smoothing, and rendering are excluded. These repeated-input measurements characterize inference cost rather than average latency over the full test set.

Appendix B Metrics and Evaluation Protocols

B.1 Evaluation Protocols

Text-to-motion.

We evaluate on 4,042 selected-caption HumanML3D test cases using the MotionStreamer MS-272 evaluator (Xiao et al., 2025). Generated motions are converted to the evaluator representation, and text–motion retrieval uses candidate batches of 32.

Motion-to-text.

We follow the TM2T protocol (Guo et al., 2022b), comprising 4,400 cases: 3,969 full motions and 431 temporal subclips. Each case has three reference captions. Linguistic metrics use the raw reference captions; semantic retrieval uses the HumanML3D matching network with candidate batches of 32.

Editing and temporal completion.

Editing follows the MotionLab protocol (Guo et al., 2025) on MotionFix, with the unchanged source included as a no-edit baseline. Temporal completion covers prediction, backcasting, in-betweening, and keyframe infilling, corresponding to the observation patterns in Table S3. Comparisons use matched sample IDs, observations, target lengths, and text conditions. Motions are converted to HumanML3D-263 where required by the evaluator.

B.2 Evaluation Metrics

Table S6 summarizes the metrics and their preferred directions. Embedding-based scores depend on the task-specific evaluator and should not be compared across different embedding spaces. For temporal completion, MPJPE and [P]-MPJPE distinguish motion reconstruction from preservation of observed frames; [P] does not denote Procrustes alignment.

Appendix C More Results

C.1 Text-to-Motion Generation

Figure S1 presents additional text-to-motion results for the shown prompts, complementing the qualitative comparisons in the main text.

C.2 Motion-to-Text Generation

Figure S2 presents additional motion-captioning examples, complementing the quantitative evaluation in the main text.

C.3 Motion Knowledge Question Answering

Table S7 presents text-only probes of motion knowledge and motion-language instruction generation. Base and ours receive the same English questions without any motion input. These examples probe motion-related knowledge and instruction generation without motion input, complementing the motion-conditioned captioning evaluation.

C.4 Temporal Completion

Table S9 reports results under four observation patterns. The 0.6B model achieves the lowest MPJPE in all four tasks, while the 1.7B model achieves the lowest FID throughout. For example, in prediction, our MPJPE reaches 7.177 compared with the best baseline’s 8.781; in keyframe infilling, our best FID is 0.286 compared with 0.358. Observed-frame preservation remains task-dependent: HY-Motion has the lowest [P]-MPJPE for prediction and Kimodo for in-betweening, whereas our models lead for backcasting and keyframe infilling. These results show complementary strengths in reconstruction and distributional quality, rather than a uniform advantage on every metric. The two model sizes also use different training data, so their comparison does not isolate model scale.

Effect of multi-task training on T2M and M2T.

Table S8 compares the main-table 0.6B model with the multi-task variant after 20k continuation steps. Adding conditional generation tasks yields a modest T2M trade-off: R@1 decreases by 1.53 percentage points, FID increases from 6.1291 to 6.6746, and MMDist increases from 13.9973 to 14.0824. Nevertheless, the multi-task model still outperforms all other HumanML3D-trained methods in Table 1 on R@1–3, FID, and MMDist, including generation-specialized models. Its M2T scores remain identical to the main-table results, consistent with keeping the understanding parameters frozen during the additional generation training.

Why report two training variants?

The main-table comparison focuses on the bidirectional T2M/M2T setting shared with unified motion–language baselines, reducing the influence of additional task-specific supervision on that comparison. The multi-task evaluation asks a complementary question: can the same architecture accommodate additional observation patterns and conditional generation objectives while retaining its core capabilities? The temporal-completion results, together with the strong T2M scores and unchanged M2T performance, support this broader task coverage without introducing task-specific generation modules. We therefore report the variants separately to make the trade-off between task breadth and T2M specialization explicit. This demonstrates extensibility across trained tasks, rather than establishing zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or distributions.
